reconcile.note: Gill reads Jesus's warning in Matthew 19:23 as targeting trust in riches, not wealth itself, so godly rich believers remain heirs of the kingdom.

discrepancy.note: Ingersoll rejects the old equation of prosperity with virtue, citing the Dives-and-Lazarus logic that wealth damns and poverty earns heaven.

quotes.text: They do not now believe that prosperity is a certain sign of wickedness, or that poverty and wretchedness are sure certificates of virtue. They are hardly convinced that Dives should have been sent to hell simply for being rich, or that Lazarus was entitled to eternal joy on account of his poverty.
quotes.attr: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), The Christian Religion, pt. III, The Works of Robert G. Ingersoll, Vol. VI (1900), on Psalm 112:3 and Matthew 19:24.

sides.snippet: Wealth and riches are in his house.
sides.verseText: Wealth and riches are in his house. His righteousness endures forever.

sides.snippet: it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God.
sides.verseText: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye, than for a rich man to enter into the Kingdom of God.\"
